newsitem.title: USA: AOL new pricing scrutinized by 15 states.
newsitem.headline: AOL new pricing scrutinized by 15 states.

text.p: America Online Inc. has received inquiries from 15 state attorneys general expressing concern about how the world's largest online service is putting its new pricing plan into effect, the company said Monday.

The inquiries also relate to how AOL is disclosing the changes to its 7 million subscribers. On Dec. 1, AOL plans to switch all subscribers to a plan charging $19.95 a month for unlimited hours of access unless members tell AOL they want another pricing option.
"The plan is fair in every sense," said an AOL spokesman at the company's headquarters in Dulles, Va. "We are bending over backwards to make sure that all the members are aware of the new pricing."
AOL currently charges $9.95 a month for five hours with an additional charge for each hour thereafter.
AOL said that it did not have a copy of the letter sent by the group of states nor did it have a list of the 15 states involved.
Late Friday, CNET, a technology news Web site, reported that New York, California, Florida, Texas and Illinois were among the states.
"What they are doing is they are going to change all these people without their consent to $19.95," said Herschel Elkins, a California senior assistant attorney general.
Elkins said the states were concerned that the practice violates "negative option" law. "You cannot tell someone they have a new service without them ordering it," he said.
The AOL spokesman said that people who want a lower-cost plan will receive a credit if they are switched to the new plan before making their wishes known.
"We have had several thousand calls about this (flat-rate pricing). Many have expressed interest in going to the unlimited pricing plan even sooner," he said.

AOL members have the option of keeping their current plan of $9.95 a month or switching to a lower-cost plan of $4.95 a month for three hours, but only if they inform AOL. Some other options, like prepaid service, are also available.

AOL said it was posting notices about the changes on its sign-on and sign-off screens. It also will mail postcards to all members informing them of the pricing switch, and AOL has a toll-free number for inquiries about the new plan.
AOL said that it is working on its response to the inquiry by the attorneys general.

AOL's embrace of the unlimited pricing option came after many Internet access providers offered unlimited Internet access for $19.95 a month. Only after Microsoft Corp. relaunched its Microsoft Network on the Internet in October at a flat rate of $19.95 a month did AOL join the trend.

In addition to Internet access, AOL offers its own content, including stock quotes, weather, online versions of newspapers and magazines, and a well-known personal finance section called The Motley Fool.
AOL mentioned the attorney generals' inquiry in one paragraph of a Securities and Exchange Commission filing Friday.

"In November, the company received communications from certain regulators concerning the company's announced plan to change its pricing," AOL said in the filing. "These regulators have expressed concern about the company's proposed method of implementing the pricing change and the adequacy of notice to the company's subscribers."
AOL said in the filing that if any of the regulators acted against AOL regarding those matters, the company would prevail.
